explanation: A prefix attaches before a word or name and adds meaning. 小 before a surname can be a familiar form of address; 第 before a number forms an ordinal such as first or second.
A suffix attaches after another element to form a word. Its function belongs to the whole expression; do not translate the suffix as if it were an independent word.
Location nouns indicate a position relative to something else. Place them after the reference noun to form a location expression, often with 在 before the whole phrase: 在桌子上 means 'on the table'.

会 before a verb can express a learned skill; 能 expresses ability or circumstances permitting an action; 可以 can express permission or possibility. 想 expresses a wish or intention, while 要 can express wanting or an intended action. Put the modal before the main verb.

A separable word contains parts that can be separated in particular grammatical constructions. Verb–object items can allow an aspect marker, quantity or modifier between their parts. Separation depends on the individual word and construction.

Use 谁 for a person, 什么 for a thing, 哪/哪些 for a choice, 哪儿/哪里 for a place, 几/多少 for a number or amount, 怎么 for a method, and 怎么样 for a condition or evaluation. Leave the question expression where its answer would go.
Personal pronouns identify the speaker, listener or another participant. They can occupy noun positions such as subject or object. Their reference depends on the people being discussed.
Demonstrative and related pronouns identify which person, thing, manner or set is meant. Before a countable noun, 这 and 那 commonly combine with a measure word: 这本书 means 'this book'.

Numerals express quantities. With a countable noun, the usual structure is number + an appropriate measure word + noun. 二 and 两 have different distributions; 两 is usual before many noun measure words.

A noun measure word connects a number or demonstrative with the noun being counted: number + measure word + noun. Choose the measure word for that noun, such as 本 for books or 辆 for vehicles. Some units measure containers, portions or physical quantities.
Time measure words express calendar units, clock time, age or duration. Interpret the unit in context: 点 marks an hour on the clock, while a duration counts how long an event lasts.

Degree adverbs indicate how strong a quality, feeling or degree is. They normally precede the adjective or relevant verb. Their individual meanings differ: 'very', 'slightly', 'more' and 'too' do not express the same degree.
都 before the predicate includes all members of a relevant set: 我们都去 means 'we are all going'. With two members it can correspond to 'both'. Identify the set that 都 ranges over.
在 or 正在 before a verb presents an action as in progress at the reference time. 我正在看书 means 'I am reading'. The reference time can be supplied by context, not only the moment of speaking.
再 before a verb requests or anticipates another occurrence: 再说一遍 means 'say it once more'. This use looks toward an additional occurrence rather than reporting a repetition that has already happened.
也 adds a parallel fact, often 'also' or 'too'; 还 can add a further item or action. Put them before the predicate: 他也去 means 'he is going too'. Their placement shows which predicate is being added.
不 negates a quality, habitual action or intention. 没(有) denies that an event occurred or that something is possessed. 不要 before an action can prohibit it: 不要说 means 'don't say it'.
在 introduces the place or time where an event is situated. A location phrase such as 在学校 normally goes before the main action: 我在学校学习 means 'I study at school'.

和 introduces a person involved together with someone in an action; 对 introduces the target of an attitude or action. In these uses, the following noun belongs to the prepositional phrase, while another word supplies the main predicate.
A conjunction joins words or phrases with equal grammatical roles. 和 links nouns or noun phrases in this use; it does not automatically replace every English 'and' between complete clauses.
的 connects a preceding modifier to a noun: 我的书 is 'my book', and 很好的书 is 'a very good book'. The noun is the head; the material before 的 identifies or describes it.

Verb-following 了 presents an action as a bounded or completed event. In 我买了一本书, 买了 presents the buying as completed. A past time is common, but 了 is chosen for the event viewpoint rather than added mechanically to every past sentence.

吗 makes a yes–no question; 吧 can soften a suggestion or express a tentative judgment; 呢 has uses including a follow-up question or emphasis on a continuing situation. Sentence-final 了 marks a new situation or change of state. The numbered labels distinguish the syllabus uses.

Interjections express reactions or manage interaction. 喂 can attract attention or answer the telephone; 啊 and 嗯 can express surprise, acknowledgment or other responses, depending on intonation and context.

A phrase combines elements according to a grammatical relationship. Coordinate phrases join equals; modifier–head phrases describe a central word; verb–object phrases pair an action with its object; subject–predicate phrases state something about a subject.

Quantity phrases combine a number with a measure word; prepositional phrases introduce a participant or circumstance; location phrases specify a position. A phrase functions as a unit inside a larger sentence.

The subject is what the sentence makes a statement about. Nouns, pronouns and noun phrases can fill this role, usually before the predicate. The grammatical subject is not necessarily the person performing an action.
The predicate says something about the subject. Chinese predicates can be verbal, adjectival or nominal. An adjective can serve as the main predicate without an English-style linking 'be'.
An object follows the verb in the basic verb–object order and identifies a participant, content or target selected by the verb. Nouns, pronouns and noun phrases can occupy this position.
An attributive modifies a noun and appears before it. The modifier may be a word, quantity phrase or larger phrase; 的 often connects the modifier to the noun when the construction requires it.
Adverbials appear before the predicate and specify circumstances such as time, place, degree or manner. Time and place expressions can function as adverbials even when they are not lexical adverbs.
An action-count complement follows the verb and states how many times the action occurs. In 看一次, 一次 counts the occurrence of looking or reading, rather than counting an object.
A simple sentence expresses one main predication. Its predicate may be verbal, adjectival or nominal. Some complete utterances do not have an explicit subject–predicate structure.
Sentence function concerns what the speaker is doing: stating something, asking, requesting or exclaiming. Function is separate from the grammatical shape of the predicate.

A question requests missing information. Yes–no questions can use 吗, information questions put a question word in the missing-information position, and A-not-A questions present positive and negative alternatives.
是 links a subject to an identity or category: 他是老师 means 'he is a teacher'. The phrase after 是 identifies or classifies the subject; ordinary adjective predicates use a different structure.
有 expresses possession: subject + 有 + possessed thing. 我有一本书 means 'I have a book'. The negative is 没有, as in 我没有车, 'I do not have a car'.
An existential or locating sentence begins with a place. 桌子上有一本书 means 'there is a book on the table'; a place + 是 + noun structure identifies what occupies that place.

A serial-verb sentence places two actions under the same subject without an overt conjunction. The first action can provide the means for the second, or movement can be followed by its purpose, as in 去学校学习, 'go to school to study'.
Some verbs take two objects, usually recipient followed by transferred thing: subject + verb + recipient + thing. 我给他一本书 means 'I give him a book'. The two objects have different roles.
A complex sentence relates two or more clauses. Chinese can leave a relationship to context instead of expressing every link with an explicit conjunction.
也 or 还 introduces an additional, parallel fact. The second clause supplies another action, quality or participant rather than a cause or consequence. Keep the connector before its predicate.

Completion aspect presents an event as a completed or bounded occurrence using 了 after the verb. Interpret its time from the sentence and context; a completion marker is not required merely because an event is in the past.

Sentence-final 了 signals that a new situation now holds or that something has changed. 下雨了 means 'it has started raining / it is raining now'. The focus is the changed situation, which differs from simply marking a verb as completed.
在/正在 before the verb indicates an action in progress; 呢 can appear at the end to reinforce the continuing situation. An appropriate context can allow 呢 without an overt 在 or 正在.
Money amounts use currency units such as 元/块 and 角/毛. 第 before a numeral marks order rather than quantity: 第一 is 'first', whereas 一 by itself is 'one'.
Chinese dates proceed from larger units to smaller ones: year, month, day. Clock time normally places the hour before the minutes, and 星期 introduces the day of the week.
面 attaches after a directional or positional element to form a location noun, such as 前面, 'in front', or 里面, 'inside'. The resulting word names a position or area.
Location nouns indicate a position relative to something else. Place them after the reference noun to form a location expression, often with 在 before the whole phrase: 在桌子上 means 'on the table'.

Verb reduplication can present an action as brief, limited or tentative. AA, A一A and ABAB are common patterns; A了A can describe a brief completed action. These patterns apply to suitable verbs rather than every verb indiscriminately.
可能 before a predicate expresses possibility: 他可能来 means 'he may come'. It presents an uncertain proposition rather than a learned skill or permission.

A separable word contains parts that can be separated in particular grammatical constructions. Verb–object items can allow an aspect marker, quantity or modifier between their parts. Separation depends on the individual word and construction.
为什么 asks for a reason and usually stands before the predicate: 你为什么不去 means 'why aren't you going?' Its answer supplies a cause or motivation.
自己 refers back to a relevant person as 'oneself' or 'one's own'. Its referent depends on the sentence and context; it does not always refer to the closest preceding noun.
这么/那么 and 这样/那样 refer to a degree or manner as 'this/that much' or 'like this/that'. 每 before an appropriate quantity or noun phrase expresses 'each/every'.
Adjective reduplication presents a vivid or fuller description, using AA or AABB with suitable adjectives. The repeated form is a construction of its own, not just an adjective repeated at random.

Numerals express quantities. With a countable noun, the usual structure is number + an appropriate measure word + noun. 二 and 两 have different distributions; 两 is usual before many noun measure words.

A noun measure word connects a number or demonstrative with the noun being counted: number + measure word + noun. Choose the measure word for that noun, such as 本 for books or 辆 for vehicles. Some units measure containers, portions or physical quantities.
次 counts occurrences of an action. 一次 means 'once' or 'one time'; it does not in itself mean one complete run from beginning to end, which 遍 can specify.
最 marks a superlative, 'most'; 好 and 多 can intensify a quality or occur in exclamatory constructions. Their effect depends on the pattern, not just a shared translation as 'very'.
一起 before a verb means that participants do an action together. 我们一起去 means 'we will go together'. The relevant participants are supplied by the subject or context.

已经 marks 'already', 还 can mean 'still', 有时(候) means 'sometimes', 正 marks an action in progress, and 快/快要 can introduce an approaching event. Identify the stage of the event before choosing the adverb.
常 and 经常 express habitual frequency: 'often'. They go before the predicate and describe repeated occurrences rather than a single completed event.
别 before a verb gives a negative instruction, 'don't'. 别走 means 'don't leave'. It is directed at preventing an action rather than reporting that the action did not occur.

再 can place one action after another, and 就 can connect a condition or preceding event to what follows. Learn the relation between the clauses rather than giving either word one fixed English equivalent.
These uses express evaluation or emphasis: 都 and 就 can mark a quantity or timing as noteworthy, while 还是 can recommend the preferable choice. Context determines the speaker's expectation.
从 introduces a starting point in time or place. 从学校出发 means 'set out from the school'; 从明天开始 means 'start from tomorrow'.
往 introduces a direction toward which something moves. 从 introduces a point of origin or a route from somewhere. They precede the relevant motion verb rather than functioning as the movement itself.

给 introduces a recipient or beneficiary; 比 introduces the comparison standard; 跟 introduces another participant or the person accompanied. The whole prepositional phrase belongs before the predicate in these uses.
因为 can introduce a reason phrase: 'because of' a circumstance. Distinguish this use from 因为 connecting an entire reason clause to another clause.
These conjunctions join words or phrases. 跟 can mean 'and' between noun phrases; distinguish this linking use from a prepositional phrase meaning 'with'.
Clause connectors make a relationship explicit: 但是 introduces contrast, 因为 introduces a reason, and 所以 introduces a result. A connector belongs with the clause whose role it marks.
地 links a manner expression to the following action: 认真地学习 means 'study conscientiously'. 得 follows a verb and introduces an evaluation or description: 说得很好 means 'speak very well'.

过 after a verb indicates prior experience of an action. 着 after a verb indicates a continuing action or state. These describe different viewpoints and cannot be selected merely because the English sentence uses a past or continuous form.

These sentence-final particles mark attitude or a sentence function. 的 can reinforce an assertion, 吧 can convey a tentative judgment, 呢 can emphasize a situation, and 啊 adds interactional or emotional coloring. Interpret the specific construction and context.

A verb–complement phrase combines an action with a following expression that adds information such as its result or direction. The complement is grammatically linked to the verb rather than being its object.

A 的 phrase can stand for a noun whose reference is understood. Serial-predicate phrases connect successive predicates; pivotal phrases share a participant that is the object of one verb and the subject of the following predicate.
A phrase can function like a noun, verb or adjective. Its function depends on the whole phrase, not simply the first word; this determines where it can occur in a sentence.
什么的 after examples makes the list non-exhaustive: 'and things like that'. It groups the named examples with other similar items understood from context.
还是……吧 recommends a preferable choice. 要/快要/就要……了 indicates an approaching event. 都……了 emphasizes a time, quantity or situation as already reached, often later or greater than expected.

A patient subject names the person or thing affected by an action. Chinese can make that affected participant the subject without an explicit passive marker when the context and construction allow it.
A noun phrase can serve as the predicate in suitable descriptive contexts such as age, date or quantity. Chinese does not require 是 before every nominal predicate.
A verb phrase or subject–predicate phrase can modify a noun before 的. 我买的书 means 'the book that I bought'; the entire phrase before 的 identifies the book.

A result complement follows the verb and says what the action achieved: 懂 indicates understanding, 完 completion, 会 acquisition of a skill, 错 an error and 好 a satisfactory result. 听懂 means 'understand through listening'.

Directional complements follow a motion or action verb. 上/下/进/出/过/回 describe the path, while 来/去 orient movement toward or away from the reference point. Compound forms combine path and orientation, as in 走进来, 'walk in toward here'.
Verb + 得 + adjective phrase evaluates how an action is performed. 他跑得很快 means 'he runs very fast'. 得 introduces the description of the running rather than a direct object.
A duration complement states how long an action lasts. An adjective followed by a quantity expression can measure the extent of a difference, as in 高三厘米, 'three centimetres taller'.
A subject–predicate phrase can itself be the predicate of a larger sentence. 他身体很好 means 'his health is very good': 他 is the overall topic/subject and 身体很好 says something about him.
还是 links the alternatives in a choice question: 你喝茶还是咖啡 means 'will you have tea or coffee?' The question asks for a choice rather than a yes–no answer.
An imperative asks, tells or urges someone to do or avoid something. The subject 'you' is often understood. 别 before a verb forms a negative instruction meaning 'don't'.

是 can introduce an explanation or characterization, including what something is made from or what kind of situation it represents. Read the full predicate after 是 to identify the characteristic being asserted.
有 can express reaching a particular extent, age, distance or quantity. The expression after 有 specifies the amount attained rather than a possessed object.

Place + verb + 着 + noun introduces something in a continuing state at that location. 桌子上放着一本书 means 'there is a book lying on the table'. The sentence presents the scene rather than narrating the act of placing it.

A比B + adjective states that A exceeds B in a quality; a following quantity can measure the difference. 没有B那么…… means 'not as ... as B'. With action quality, 得 introduces the description being compared.
This 是……的 construction presents a past event and focuses on a detail such as when, where, how or by whom it happened. 我是昨天来的 means 'I came yesterday', with 昨天 as the focused time.
In a pivotal construction, the object of 请/叫/让 is also the understood subject of the next verb. 我请他来 means 'I invite/ask him to come': 他 is both the person asked and the person who comes.
Verb + 给 + recipient + thing identifies the recipient of a transfer. 我送给他一本书 means 'I give him a book as a gift'. The person and the thing fill different object roles.
（是）……还是…… presents alternatives and asks which applies. The alternatives can be clauses rather than only noun phrases. Do not use 和 when the speaker is asking the listener to choose.
虽然 introduces a conceded fact and 但是 introduces a contrasting fact: 'although ... , ...'. Both connectors may appear in Chinese; the contrast is between the two clauses.
因为 introduces the reason; 所以 introduces its consequence: 'because ... , therefore ...'. The reason and result have different roles, and Chinese permits both markers in the same sentence.
一……就…… connects the onset or occurrence of the first event with an immediate or regular consequence: 'as soon as ... , ...'. It need not describe a one-time past event.
着 presents a state or activity as continuing at the reference time. 门开着 means 'the door is open'; the sentence describes the continuing state rather than the event of opening it.

过 after a verb says that the subject has had that experience before the reference time. 我去过北京 means 'I have been to Beijing'. It does not by itself give the exact occasion or imply the situation continues now.

A number plus measure word can identify an ordered unit in an appropriate sequence. 几 expresses an unspecified small number; 多 after a number or quantity expression means an amount over that quantity. The placement of 多 affects what amount is being approximated.
老 before a surname can be a familiar form of address. Its interpersonal meaning depends on the relationship and context; it does not simply state the person's age.

家 can form names for specialists or practitioners, 员 for members or people in a role, and 子 forms many nouns. These are word-building uses, so interpret the whole word rather than translating each suffix literally.
Location nouns indicate a position relative to something else. Place them after the reference noun to form a location expression, often with 在 before the whole phrase: 在桌子上 means 'on the table'.

需要 expresses need; 该 and 应该 express what should be done; 愿意 expresses willingness; 得, pronounced děi, expresses necessity. Put these before the main predicate, keeping the intended strength and meaning distinct.

A separable word contains parts that can be separated in particular grammatical constructions. Verb–object items can allow an aspect marker, quantity or modifier between their parts. Separation depends on the individual word and construction.

怎样 asks 'how'. Question pronouns also have non-question uses: with 都 they can refer to any/all members, and repeated question words can link corresponding choices. An indefinite use refers to someone or something without asking for its identity.
别人 means 'other people / someone else'. 咱们 means 'we/us' including the listener. Identify who is included rather than translating every first-person plural pronoun identically.
别的 and 其他 refer to other members beyond those already mentioned. They can modify a noun or refer to an understood one, with the form of the whole phrase determining whether 的 is required.

A noun measure word connects a number or demonstrative with the noun being counted: number + measure word + noun. Choose the measure word for that noun, such as 本 for books or 辆 for vehicles. Some units measure containers, portions or physical quantities.

These action units differ: 遍 counts a complete run through an action, 回 an occurrence, 声 a vocal or sound occurrence, and 口 can count a bite or mouthful. The measure word specifies the action unit being counted.
Repeating a measure word expresses distribution over all members: 个个 means 'every one', and 张张 means 'every sheet'. The measure word still has to suit the noun being counted.

比较 means 'relatively', 更 'more', 特别 'especially/particularly', 挺 'quite', and 有些 'somewhat'. 越 introduces an increasing degree, while 极 can occur in the post-adjectival pattern 极了. Learn each pattern's position.

Scope adverbs specify which members or how much of a set a statement covers. They normally come before the predicate and take their scope from context; distinguish totality, restriction and togetherness.
刚/刚刚 mean 'just', 马上 'immediately/soon', 先 'first', 一直 'continuously/all along', and 一会儿 can express a short interval. 才 can emphasize lateness or that an event occurs only after a condition is met.
总/总是 and 常常 describe habitual recurrence. 又 reports a further occurrence that has happened or is being presented as realized; compare 再, which often anticipates another occurrence.
一边……一边…… presents two actions occurring concurrently under a relevant participant: 'do one thing while doing another'. Each 一边 belongs to its own action phrase.

大概 expresses probability, 好像 an impression, 一定 strong certainty or determination, 必须 necessity, 几乎 'almost', and 差不多 approximate similarity or amount. Match the word to the speaker's degree of commitment.

Attitude adverbs add the speaker's judgment, emphasis, expectation or evaluation to a statement. They normally precede the relevant predicate. The basic event may stay the same while the speaker's stance changes.
不必 and 不用 before a predicate mean 'there is no need to'. They deny necessity rather than prohibiting the action or asserting that it did not occur.

为 introduces the person or cause served by an action; 向 can introduce a person addressed or approached; 关于 introduces a topic. The following noun is the object of the preposition, not automatically the object of the main verb.
A direction or route preposition introduces where movement is headed or the path it follows. Put the phrase before the motion verb: 往学校走 means 'walk toward the school'.

为了 introduces an intended purpose, 'in order to / for the sake of'. 为 can introduce a purpose, beneficiary or cause depending on the construction. Separate the intended goal from the main action taken to achieve it.

把 introduces a known or identifiable affected object before the verb. 被 marks a passive relationship and can introduce the agent. The following verb phrase describes what happens to the affected participant.
根据 introduces evidence or a basis for an action or inference, 'according to / on the basis of'. The phrase normally precedes the conclusion or action based on it.
或 and 或者 introduce alternatives and usually mean 'or' in statements. For a direct question asking the listener to choose between alternatives, 还是 is the usual connector.

These conjunctions connect clauses and indicate a logical relationship such as addition, condition, contrast, cause or result. Their positions and possible partners are part of the construction shown below.
的话 after a clause or phrase can set it up as a condition or topic: 'if ...' or 'as for ...'. In a conditional pattern, a following 就 clause commonly supplies the consequence.

Appositive phrases place two expressions with the same reference together. Verb–complement phrases add result or related information after a verb. Repeating number + measure-word units can express a sequence or distribution, such as 'one ... after another'.
不A不B is a conventional four-character frame often expressing 'neither A nor B' or a combined negative description. Its interpretation depends on the particular words in the two slots.

不一会儿 means 'before long'; 看来 and 看起来/看上去 present an appearance or inference; 在……看来 gives a viewpoint. 越来越 means 'increasingly', 一般来说 'generally speaking', and 不怎么样 gives a negative or lukewarm evaluation.

除了……以外 can add to or exclude a set; 还/也 versus 都 helps establish the reading. 对……来说 sets a viewpoint; 从……起 sets a starting point. 一……也/都不/没 and 一点儿也不 emphasize a zero amount or degree. 越……越…… means 'the more ... , the more ...'. 以前/以后 locate events before/after a reference; 该……了 says it is time for something. X什么 can reject the appropriateness of X; 在……上/下/中 sets a domain, condition or process.

A verb phrase, adjective phrase or subject–predicate phrase can itself be the subject: the sentence then says something about that activity, quality or proposition. The subject's role belongs to the whole phrase.

A noun can have several attributive modifiers. Work out which modifier describes the head noun and which modifies another modifier. Possession, demonstratives, quantity and descriptive phrases occupy different positions in the noun phrase.
到/住/走/上 after a verb can express an achieved result rather than a separate action. The combination determines the result: 找到 is 'find', 记住 is 'remember firmly', and 拿走 is 'take away'.

Directional forms can acquire extended meanings: 出/起/下 may mark a result, 上/起来 the start of an action, and 下去/下来 its continuation or development. Interpret the verb–complement combination, not only literal movement.

Put 得 or 不 between a verb and its result/directional complement to express whether that result is attainable: 看得懂 means 'can understand by reading', 看不懂 'cannot understand by reading'. This is a potential construction, distinct from evaluating how well someone reads.

A post-adjectival or post-verbal complement can intensify degree. 得很 means 'very'; 极了 and 坏了 mark a high or extreme degree with suitable predicates. Their position after the predicate differs from pre-predicate 很.

A time-quantity complement can measure the interval since an action ended or since an event occurred. Determine whether the phrase measures the action's duration or the time elapsed afterward; the surrounding construction establishes that distinction.
怎样 before a verb asks about the method or way of doing it: 'how does one ...?' The answer supplies the manner or procedure, not simply a yes or no.
不是……吗？ can be a rhetorical reminder: 'isn't it the case that ...?' The speaker often treats the proposition as already known or expects agreement rather than neutrally requesting new information.

把 puts an identifiable affected object before a verb phrase describing its handling or outcome. The predicate can specify a resulting location, recipient, result, direction or state. In 把书放在桌子上, the book is the affected object and its resulting location is on the table.

In a 被 passive, the subject is affected by the action. An agent may follow 被, or be omitted: 书被拿走了 means 'the book was taken away'. The remainder of the predicate expresses the action and its relevant outcome or other information.
Verb1 + 着 + verb2 can present the first action or posture as accompanying the second: 笑着说 means 'speak while smiling'. Both activities are associated with the same relevant participant.

更/还 can strengthen a 比 comparison. 跟……一样 expresses equality, optionally in a stated quality. 不比 means 'not more ... than', which differs from asserting 'less than'. A quantity phrase can measure how much more/less or earlier/later an action occurs.

A place-first sentence can announce an appearance or disappearance there. The following verb plus result/directional information describes what enters, appears, leaves or vanishes; the person or thing is introduced after that predicate.

This 是……的 pattern reinforces the speaker's judgment or assurance rather than focusing on the time or manner of a past event. It can emphasize an opinion, prediction or attitude; context distinguishes it from the event-focus pattern.

When a verb has an object and also takes a complement, Chinese can repeat the verb: subject + verb + object + verb + complement. 他唱歌唱得很好 means 'he sings very well'. The second verb carries the complement.
先 introduces the first step, and 再/然后 the following step: 'first ... , then ...'. The ordering is between actions or stages, rather than a comparison of their frequency.
或者……或者…… presents alternatives in a statement: 'either ... or ...'. It does not itself ask the listener to choose, unlike a direct alternative question with 还是.
一会儿……一会儿…… alternates between situations; 又……又…… combines two qualities or actions; 一边……一边…… expresses simultaneous actions. These patterns organize parallel information in different ways.
不但……而且…… means 'not only ... but also ...'. The second clause adds a further point, often stronger or more informative than the first.
虽然……可是…… concedes the first fact and contrasts it with the second: 'although ... , ...'. The second clause often carries the speaker's main point.
如果……就…… and ……的话，就…… establish a hypothetical condition and its consequence: 'if ... , then ...'. They do not assert that the condition has actually been met.
只有……才…… states a necessary condition: 'only if ...'. 只要……就…… states a sufficient condition: 'as long as ...'. Reversing them changes the logical relationship.
为了 introduces a purpose: 'in order to ...'. The other clause gives the action taken toward that goal. A purpose is intended, and need not already have been achieved.

A compact sequence can place 了 on a preceding event and optionally 就 before the following action. The context establishes an event sequence or a consequence after completion, rather than requiring an overt conjunction for every link.
大概 before a quantity gives an approximate amount. Adjacent numerals such as 两三 can express an estimate, 'two or three'. The estimate is a range or approximation rather than an exact arithmetic sum.
敢 before a verb expresses having the courage or willingness to risk an action. 不敢 means 'dare not / not have the courage to'; it differs from being physically unable to do it.

各 refers distributively to members or kinds, 各位 addresses a group respectfully, 各种 means 'various kinds', 任何 means 'any' without restriction, and 此 is a formal 'this'. Choose the form that fits the following noun or reference.

A noun measure word connects a number or demonstrative with the noun being counted: number + measure word + noun. Choose the measure word for that noun, such as 本 for books or 辆 for vehicles. Some units measure containers, portions or physical quantities.
场 counts an event or session, 顿 commonly a meal or an episode of an action such as scolding, and 趟 a journey or trip. The classifier determines what constitutes one unit of the event.

Degree adverbs indicate how strong a quality, feeling or degree is. They normally precede the adjective or relevant verb. Their individual meanings differ: 'very', 'slightly', 'more' and 'too' do not express the same degree.

Scope adverbs specify which members or how much of a set a statement covers. They normally come before the predicate and take their scope from context; distinguish totality, restriction and togetherness.

Time adverbs place an event relative to a time or indicate its stage: already, still, just, soon or throughout. They generally come before the verb phrase; choose according to whether the event has begun, continues or is expected.

Frequency adverbs describe how often an event happens or whether it happens again. Place them before the predicate. Habitual frequency, a repeated past event and another future occurrence require different words.
Manner adverbs describe how an action is carried out, such as deliberately, personally, secretly or mutually. They normally precede the verb phrase rather than appearing after the object.
却 introduces a contrast with an expectation or another fact. It normally occurs after the subject and before the predicate of its own clause, often corresponding to 'yet' or an emphatic 'but'.

也许 expresses uncertainty, 'perhaps'. 恐怕 can express an unwelcome likelihood or a cautious assessment, often 'I'm afraid / probably'. They qualify the proposition rather than identifying the event's date.

Attitude adverbs add the speaker's judgment, emphasis, expectation or evaluation to a statement. They normally precede the relevant predicate. The basic event may stay the same while the speaker's stance changes.
自/由 can introduce an origin, 当 a relevant time or occasion, 随着 a developing circumstance, and 等 a time reached after waiting for an event. Read the phrase as the setting for the main predicate.

将 can introduce an affected object in a formal 把-like construction. 由 introduces the responsible agent; 叫 and 让 can mark a passive agent in appropriate constructions. The grammatical role depends on the construction, not just the word's everyday meaning.
由于 introduces a cause, often before the main consequence. It can introduce a reason phrase or a clause; here the syllabus singles out its prepositional cause-introducing use.

This prepositional phrase identifies the person, thing or topic toward which an action or attitude is directed. It usually precedes the main predicate. The preposition determines whether the relationship is to, for, with, toward or regarding someone or something.
作为 means 'in the capacity of / as'; 按 and 按照 introduce a rule, instruction or basis followed by an action. The following noun phrase supplies the role or standard.

These conjunctions connect words or phrases with equal roles. The listed forms differ in register and relationship, including addition or contrast; identify the units being joined before choosing the conjunction.

These conjunctions connect clauses and indicate a logical relationship such as addition, condition, contrast, cause or result. Their positions and possible partners are part of the construction shown below.

等 can mark an unfinished list; 者 can form an expression for a person with a stated role or property; 之 links elements in mainly written expressions. 就是 has an emphasizing or focusing use in the constructions concerned.

Interjections express reactions or manage interaction. 喂 can attract attention or answer the telephone; 啊 and 嗯 can express surprise, acknowledgment or other responses, depending on intonation and context.
An adjective may be inserted between a number and its measure word to describe the unit or portion: 一大杯水 is 'a large glass of water'. 大 describes the size of the glassful being counted.

These four-character frames build conventional combined descriptions. 一A一B pairs units or actions, 无A无B combines two absences, and 有A有B combines two present qualities. The actual words in the slots determine the expression's meaning.

来得及/来不及 says there is/is not enough time to do something. 有的是 means there is plenty; 说不定 expresses uncertainty; 不怎么 reduces a quality or frequency. 就是说/这就是说 introduces a restatement: 'that is to say'.

一+measure word+比+一+measure word compares successive units; 在……方面 sets a domain; 够……的 emphasizes degree; 拿……来说 introduces an example. 再也不/没 means 'never again / no longer'; 怎么也不/没 emphasizes failure under any attempt. 为了……而…… marks purpose. 动词+一X是一X stresses taking each unit as it comes. （没）有什么好X的 evaluates whether X is worthwhile. X是X，Y是Y separates two matters. X也得X，不X也得X says X is unavoidable; X就是了 offers a straightforward instruction. 还X呢 can reject an assumption; 你X你的吧 leaves someone to their own action. 让/叫你X你就X urges compliance; 怎么也得X insists on a minimum obligation. X就X吧 accepts a concession; X是X concedes X before a qualification supplied by context.
死了 and 厉害 after suitable adjectives or psychological predicates express a very high degree. They often correspond to 'extremely' rather than literal death or physical severity.

Verb + 得了/不了 expresses whether an action can be accomplished or coped with; 了 is read liǎo in this complement. 吃不了 means 'cannot eat/finish/manage it', with the precise limitation supplied by context.

难道……吗？ presents a rhetorical challenge or expected answer. Question words can also form rhetorical questions whose answer the speaker treats as obvious; interpret the question's discourse role, not just its surface punctuation.

These 把 patterns describe the handling of an affected object using verb repetition, an aspect-marked action, an action count, a duration or another modifier. The object is placed before a predicate that supplies relevant information about what is done to it.

叫 or 让 can introduce the agent in a passive sentence: the subject is the affected participant, and the noun after 叫/让 identifies who acts. The same words can express causation elsewhere, so identify the full construction.

A pivotal participant links two predicates. In praise/criticism patterns, the second predicate gives what the person is praised or criticized for; naming/selection patterns assign a role; 使/让 patterns describe a caused action or state.
A不如B states that A falls short of B, optionally in a stated quality. 跟……相比 sets the comparison standard, 'compared with ...', after which the sentence gives the comparison itself.
Two negations can combine to affirm or emphasize a conclusion. 不得不 means 'have no choice but to', for example. Work out the scope of each negation instead of deleting them mechanically.
不是……而是…… replaces an incorrect characterization with the correct one. 既……又/也…… combines two facts. 一方面……另一方面…… presents different sides or considerations.
首先 introduces the first point or step; 其次 introduces another point, while 然后 introduces a following step. 于是 presents what follows as a development or consequence of the preceding situation.
甚至 adds an extreme or noteworthy case. 不仅/不光……还/而且…… adds a further point; 并且 joins an additional statement. 连……都/也…… can establish a strong case before an even stronger conclusion.
不是……就是…… narrows the possibilities to two: 'if it isn't A, it is B / either A or B'. The pattern does not present an open-ended list.
尽管……但是/可是…… concedes a fact before a contrast; 然而 introduces a more written-style 'however'; 不过 adds a limiting qualification. X是X，就是/不过…… admits X while drawing attention to a drawback or exception.
要是……就…… sets up an 'if ... then ...' relationship. 否则 introduces what will follow if the relevant condition is not met: 'otherwise'. Track which possibility each clause describes.
不管/无论……都/也…… means that the result holds regardless of the alternatives in the first clause. The first clause often contains a question word or alternatives rather than asserting just one fixed fact.
既然 treats the first fact as accepted and draws a conclusion with 就: 'since ...'. 由于……因此…… states a cause and resulting consequence in a more explicit or written-style form.
好 before a following clause can introduce the purpose enabled by an action, 'so that ...'. It is not an adjective meaning 'good' in this use.
即使/就是……也…… concedes a hypothetical or extreme condition and says the result still holds: 'even if ...'. It differs from 虽然, which normally concedes a fact presented as actual.

A condensed sentence can leave the relationship between clauses unmarked when context makes it clear. 不……也…… can say the second situation holds even without the first action or condition; the precise interpretation depends on the predicate and context.

来 and approximators such as 大约/左右/前后 give estimates. Decimals, fractions, percentages and multiples have distinct reading patterns; for fractions, the denominator precedes 分之 and the numerator follows it.
头 is a noun-forming suffix in words such as 石头. Its word-building use does not independently mean a person's 'head'; learn the resulting noun as a whole.
彼此 refers mutually to the parties, 如此 means 'like this / so', and 本 can refer to 'this/current' in formal noun phrases. Their references come from the participants or current context.

A noun measure word connects a number or demonstrative with the noun being counted: number + measure word + noun. Choose the measure word for that noun, such as 本 for books or 辆 for vehicles. Some units measure containers, portions or physical quantities.
眼 can count a look or glance in an action quantity expression: 看一眼 means 'take a look'. The unit being counted is the act of looking, not a physical eye.

Degree adverbs indicate how strong a quality, feeling or degree is. They normally precede the adjective or relevant verb. Their individual meanings differ: 'very', 'slightly', 'more' and 'too' do not express the same degree.

Time adverbs place an event relative to a time or indicate its stage: already, still, just, soon or throughout. They generally come before the verb phrase; choose according to whether the event has begun, continues or is expected.

Frequency adverbs describe how often an event happens or whether it happens again. Place them before the predicate. Habitual frequency, a repeated past event and another future occurrence require different words.
尽量 before a verb means to do as much as possible or make the best effort; 亲自 means to do it personally. The adverb describes how the action is carried out.
便 can link a preceding condition or event to its consequence, similar to a written-style 就. 一旦 introduces the triggering condition, 'once', whose consequence is commonly introduced by 就.
似乎 and 仿佛 present something as apparent, 'seemingly / as if'. They signal an impression or comparison rather than an unqualified assertion that the situation is so.

Attitude adverbs add the speaker's judgment, emphasis, expectation or evaluation to a statement. They normally precede the relevant predicate. The basic event may stay the same while the speaker's stance changes.
自从 introduces the starting event or time from which a later situation has held: 'since ...'. The rest of the sentence supplies the development or continuing situation after that starting point.
朝 introduces a direction toward a place or person. 沿(着) introduces the path followed, 'along'. Both form phrases preceding the relevant movement or action.

替 introduces the person for whom or in whose place an action is done; 同 can mean 'with'; 较 introduces a standard of comparison in a mainly written register. Each selects a different relationship to the main predicate.

凭 identifies the means or qualification relied on; 据 and 依据 identify evidence or a basis. The following phrase supplies the support for the action or conclusion, 'by / on the basis of / according to'.

These conjunctions connect words or phrases with equal roles. The listed forms differ in register and relationship, including addition or contrast; identify the units being joined before choosing the conjunction.
从而 introduces a resulting development, 可见 a conclusion inferred from evidence, 假如 a hypothesis, and 总之 a summary. Identify the logical role of the following clause before choosing the connector.
似的 attaches to an expression to form a comparison, 'as if / like'. The resulting phrase can describe the manner or appearance of an action or state.

A来A去 expresses repeated movement or repeated consideration, A着A着 an activity continuing until a development occurs, 没A没B a paired negative description, and 说A就A prompt action or change following the stated idea.

不得了 expresses a high degree; 用不着 means 'no need to'; 从……来看 sets a perspective; A的A，B的B distributes people or things into different activities. （自）……以来 marks a period since a starting point; 由……组成 means 'be made up of'. X也不是，Y也不是 rejects both options, while X也X不得，Y也Y不得 describes being unable to do either.

X是它，Y也是它 can identify the same source of different outcomes; X着也是X着 treats a current state as an opportunity to act. 不管怎样说 means 'in any case'; 真有你的 conveys a marked reaction to someone's conduct. X什么X rejects X; 什么X不X（的） dismisses the distinction. 不X白不X urges taking an available opportunity. X来X去，都是…… evaluates repeated effort as leading to the same result. 动词+什么就是什么 makes the outcome follow whatever is said or done.

Several adverbials can occur before one predicate, describing time, place, participants, manner or other circumstances. Work out their scopes: one may modify the entire event while another describes only how the action is performed.
Verb + 得/不得 can express whether an action is possible, permissible or bearable in the construction concerned. The negative 不得 can convey a restriction, not merely a lack of physical skill.
得不得了 after an adjective or psychological predicate expresses an extreme degree, 'extremely'. The 得 phrase is the complement of that predicate rather than a separate object.

Directional complements can describe a developing state: 下来 can mark settling into a state, 下去 its continuation, 起来 its onset or emerging impression, and 过来/过去 a transition relative to a reference state. The verb/adjective combination determines the reading.

A 得 complement can be a verb phrase, a whole subject–predicate phrase or a fixed expression. It describes the degree, state or consequence associated with the preceding predicate, rather than just naming its object.

有着 expresses the existence or possession of a characteristic in an expanded written-style predicate. In verb + 有 combinations, the predicate can state that something is attached, recorded or present, such as 写有, 'have written on it'.

把 can precede an affected object followed by 一 + verb for a compact completed action. Another pattern uses a second object after the verb to express a role, identity or resulting relationship involving the 把 object.

Two verb phrases under one subject can stand in a causal, contrasting or conditional relationship without an explicit conjunction. Determine the relationship from their meanings and context rather than assuming every serial predicate describes chronological steps.
A + adjective + B + quantity complement states how much A exceeds B in a quality without an overt 比. The quantity measures the difference, for example an age, length or height difference.
给 can occur before the main verb in an expanded 被/叫/让 passive. The subject remains the affected participant; the extra 给 belongs to the passive construction rather than necessarily meaning 'give'.
便 before the second predicate presents an event that follows from the first situation, often 'then / thereupon'. It is common in written or more formal narration.
或是……或是…… presents possible alternatives, 'either ... or ...'. The sentence proposes alternatives rather than necessarily asking a direct choice question.
一旦 marks a triggering event, 假如 a hypothesis, and 万一 an unwanted possibility. Their consequence often uses 就. 要不然/不然 introduces what would happen otherwise if the relevant condition were not met.

因而 introduces a resulting consequence; 可见 introduces an inference supported by the preceding information. Distinguish what actually follows as a result from what the speaker concludes from the evidence.
哪怕……也…… means 'even if ...', often selecting a minimal or extreme condition. The second clause states what will still hold or what the speaker remains committed to.

不但不/没有……反而…… says that an expected outcome fails to occur and the opposite happens instead. 不是……还/还是…… can reject one characterization while insisting on a further or continuing fact; context supplies the contrast.
为的是 introduces the purpose motivating the preceding action: 'the purpose is to / in order to'. The purpose clause explains what the action is intended to achieve.
没有……就没有…… makes one condition necessary for another outcome. 不……不…… can express dependence through paired negatives. 再……也…… says an outcome holds even at a high or extreme degree: 'however ...'.
These productive prefix-like elements come before a base and contribute a general meaning, such as super-, multi-, anti-, non-, sub- or quasi-. Their interpretation depends on the whole word.

These productive suffix-like elements attach after a base to form terms for a process, style, type, property or other category. Learn the meaning of the complete word along with the contribution of the suffix.

人家 can refer to another person or to other people, often with a conversational stance of comparison or distance. It can also be a context-dependent way to refer to oneself. Identify the intended person from the conversation.

A noun measure word connects a number or demonstrative with the noun being counted: number + measure word + noun. Choose the measure word for that noun, such as 本 for books or 辆 for vehicles. Some units measure containers, portions or physical quantities.
番 counts a bout or substantial instance of an activity, such as an explanation or effort. The unit is an episode of action rather than a simple count of physical objects.

Degree adverbs indicate how strong a quality, feeling or degree is. They normally precede the adjective or relevant verb. Their individual meanings differ: 'very', 'slightly', 'more' and 'too' do not express the same degree.

Scope adverbs specify which members or how much of a set a statement covers. They normally come before the predicate and take their scope from context; distinguish totality, restriction and togetherness.

Time adverbs place an event relative to a time or indicate its stage: already, still, just, soon or throughout. They generally come before the verb phrase; choose according to whether the event has begun, continues or is expected.
一再 and 再三 emphasize repeated occurrence, often several times. They normally precede the verb and can emphasize persistence, insistence or repeated attempts.
Manner adverbs describe how an action is carried out, such as deliberately, personally, secretly or mutually. They normally precede the verb phrase rather than appearing after the object.
未必 means 'not necessarily'. It weakens a claim of certainty; it does not assert that the opposite is certainly true.

Attitude adverbs add the speaker's judgment, emphasis, expectation or evaluation to a statement. They normally precede the relevant predicate. The basic event may stay the same while the speaker's stance changes.
于 is a mainly written preposition that can introduce a time, place or other relation selected by the construction. Its English rendering may be 'at', 'in' or 'on', so interpret the phrase in context.
至于 introduces a new topic, 'as for / as to'. It sets that topic apart for comment, often after discussion of a different one.
因 introduces a cause or reason in a mainly written register. The phrase supplies why the event or judgment arises, not the intended goal of an action.
除 introduces an excluded member or a set apart from the others. The rest of the construction determines whether the meaning is 'except for' or 'in addition to'.
不料 introduces an unexpected development, 'unexpectedly / contrary to expectations'. It marks the following outcome as surprising relative to what preceded it.

所 before a verb can help form a nominal modifier or nominal expression, especially in written language. 所说的 means 'what is said / the ... that is said', with the referent supplied by the construction.

啦 often fuses the effects of 了 and 啊 in conversation, while 嘛 can mark a fact as evident or remind the listener of it. Interpret the speaker's stance and intonation rather than translating them as content words.
也好 can accept a choice or treat it as an acceptable possibility, 'that is fine too'. In paired structures it can allow either of two alternatives.

A这A那 can describe repeatedly doing A in relation to different matters, sometimes with an evaluative tone. 左A右B pairs actions or considerations in different directions. The words inserted in these conventional frames determine the full meaning.

好(不)容易 can express accomplishing something with difficulty, depending on the construction. 那倒(也)是 concedes another person's point. 算了 and 得了 can dismiss a matter or tell someone to stop pursuing it; tone and context determine the force.

A一+measure word，B一+measure word and 东一A，西一A distribute actions or things. 到……为止 sets an endpoint. X到Y头上来 means X has reached or fallen on Y. 不X不……，一X…… contrasts not doing X with the marked result once it happens. 好你个X and 看/瞧把……X得 express evaluation. 早也不X，晚也不X criticizes the timing. 放着X不Y describes neglecting an available X. X了就X了 accepts a fait accompli; 这也不X那也不Y rejects options. X归X，Y归Y keeps two facts separate; 看你X的 evaluates someone's resulting state or behavior.
透 after a suitable verb or adjective indicates thoroughness or an extreme degree, often followed by 了. The combination can mean 'completely' or 'through and through', depending on the predicate.

Advanced 把 sentences can have a nonhuman cause as the subject, or place the participant that performs the following action after 把. Identify the cause, affected participant and resulting event from the whole construction instead of assigning roles solely from word order.
一时……一时…… alternates between temporary situations, roughly 'at one moment ... , at another ...'. The relationship is alternating states rather than two permanent qualities.
要么……要么…… presents two alternatives, 'either ... or ...'. It can suggest a choice between them or state the possible outcomes, depending on context.
虽……但/可/却/也…… concedes one fact while maintaining a contrasting point. 虽 is a shorter and often more written-style form of 虽然.
凡是……都…… applies a result to every case meeting the condition. 除非……才…… restricts an outcome to an exceptional necessary condition; 除非……否则…… gives the outcome that holds unless that condition is met.
就算……也…… concedes a hypothetical condition: 'even supposing ... , still ...'. The condition need not be actual for the speaker to maintain the result.
以便 introduces the intended outcome made possible by a preceding action, 'so that / in order that'. It commonly appears in explanatory or written-style sentences.
后 can build terms for a later or post- period; 亲 can indicate a pro- orientation or close/direct relationship depending on the word. Interpret these prefix-like uses as parts of the complete term.

These suffix-like elements form families of words: 观 can indicate an outlook, 界 a community or field, 坛 a sphere, 制 a system, and 然 an adverbial or descriptive form. 鬼 and 为 have particular word-building uses that depend on the base.

These predicates express wishes, judgments, justification or formal actions. 巴不得/恨不得 express strong wishes; 并非 denies an identification; 犯得着/犯不着 evaluates whether something is warranted; 予以 formally introduces an action given to a target. They do not all take the same complement structure.
我 can occur in conventional formal expressions referring to 'our' side, organization or country. Its reference comes from the represented group, not only the individual speaker.
Demonstrative and related pronouns identify which person, thing, manner or set is meant. Before a countable noun, 这 and 那 commonly combine with a measure word: 这本书 means 'this book'.

Question words stand where the missing information belongs: 谁 asks who, 什么 asks what, 哪里 asks where, and 怎么 asks how. Chinese normally keeps them in that position rather than moving them to the front as English often does.
Quantity pronouns refer to amounts or unspecified numbers. 几许 and 若干 belong mainly to formal or written language; use the expression that fits the noun and context.

A noun measure word connects a number or demonstrative with the noun being counted: number + measure word + noun. Choose the measure word for that noun, such as 本 for books or 辆 for vehicles. Some units measure containers, portions or physical quantities.

An action measure word counts occurrences or units of an action rather than objects. It normally follows the verb in a quantity phrase; the particular measure word tells what counts as one occurrence.
Compound measure words combine two units into one measure, such as person-times or passenger-kilometres. The resulting unit measures combined activity rather than just a number of individual objects.

Degree adverbs indicate how strong a quality, feeling or degree is. They normally precede the adjective or relevant verb. Their individual meanings differ: 'very', 'slightly', 'more' and 'too' do not express the same degree.

Scope adverbs specify which members or how much of a set a statement covers. They normally come before the predicate and take their scope from context; distinguish totality, restriction and togetherness.

Time adverbs place an event relative to a time or indicate its stage: already, still, just, soon or throughout. They generally come before the verb phrase; choose according to whether the event has begun, continues or is expected.

Frequency adverbs describe how often an event happens or whether it happens again. Place them before the predicate. Habitual frequency, a repeated past event and another future occurrence require different words.
Manner adverbs describe how an action is carried out, such as deliberately, personally, secretly or mutually. They normally precede the verb phrase rather than appearing after the object.
不见得 means 'not necessarily'; 绝不 is emphatic 'absolutely not'; 无从 means there is no way or basis to act; 无须 means 'need not'; 无可 introduces the absence of a possibility; 勿 is a formal prohibition.

Attitude adverbs add the speaker's judgment, emphasis, expectation or evaluation to a statement. They normally precede the relevant predicate. The basic event may stay the same while the speaker's stance changes.
A judgment adverb establishes or identifies something in a statement. 乃 is a formal or literary expression used for identification, often corresponding to 'is' or 'is precisely'.
打 can introduce a starting point in time or place in a colloquial prepositional use. It corresponds to 'from/since' in that construction rather than the ordinary verb 'hit'.

当着 introduces the person in whose presence an action takes place. 就 can introduce the topic, aspect or issue under discussion in a formal prepositional use, rather than expressing time or immediate consequence.

本着 introduces a guiding principle; 基于 and 鉴于 introduce a basis or circumstance considered; 经 indicates passage through a process; 依 means 'according to'. These phrases establish the grounds for the main action or conclusion.

鉴于 introduces a fact taken into consideration, 况且 adds a further argument, 免得 and 以防 introduce an outcome to be avoided, and 若/倘若 introduce a hypothesis. Choose the connector according to the logical relationship.

path: 连接词或词组以及分句或句子
explanation: These connectors can join phrases or clauses. 加之 adds a further circumstance, 乃至 extends the range to a further or extreme case, and 且 adds a coordinated fact in a mainly written register.

罢了 limits a claim, 'merely / that's all'; 也罢 accepts or sets aside an alternative; 矣 is a literary sentence particle often marking a changed or completed situation. These differ substantially in register and force.

These conventional four-character frames combine meanings across slots. 爱A不A can dismiss whether A is done; 半A半B combines partial qualities; 不A而B expresses B without A; 连A带B includes both; 无A不B can generalize B across all cases. Others describe alternation, scattered action or paired qualities. Their full meaning depends on the established words filling the frame.

Discourse markers manage how an utterance relates to the conversation rather than naming an event. They can introduce candor, reformulate a point, concede, return to a topic, draw a conclusion or express a reaction. Examples include 换句话说, 'in other words', and 总而言之, 'to sum up'.

These fixed frames encode evaluations and discourse relations. X到这个地步/份上 and X得要命/要死 emphasize an extreme point or degree; X都不/没X emphasizes not even doing X. X也好Y也罢 accepts alternatives; 别提有多……了 intensifies a quality. 不亚于 means 'not inferior to'; 仅次于 means 'second only to'. 动不动就 describes easy or frequent triggering. 何至于/谈何 challenge whether something is warranted or achievable. 看在……面子上 appeals to a relationship; 视……而定 makes a decision depend on a condition. 没什么好V的 dismisses the value of V; 有/没什么V头儿 evaluates its interest or prospect. 无非/不过/只是……罢了/而已 limits a claim to 'merely'. 因……而…… gives a cause, 在……之余 adds activity outside the main occupation, and 值此……之际 introduces a formal occasion. The other frames use their repeated slots to express distribution, insistence, choice or an emotional judgment.
An adjective followed by 于 or 过 can introduce a comparison standard in a more compact, often written-style pattern. A高于B means 'A is higher than B'. The noun after 于/过 is the comparison standard.
一来……二来……三来…… and 一则……二则……三则…… enumerate parallel reasons or considerations. Their ordering structures the argument; it need not be a chronological sequence of events.
所谓……就是…… introduces a term or characterization and then explains it: 'what is called ... is ...'. The second clause identifies what the expression means in the discussion.
或……或…… lists alternatives. 宁可/宁愿……也不…… expresses a preference for one outcome over an avoided one. 与其……宁愿/宁可…… compares an undesirable option with the preferred alternative.
X倒是X了 admits that X occurred before a qualification; 别看…… warns against drawing the expected conclusion from appearances; 虽说……但/可…… concedes a fact before a contrasting point.
无论……与否都…… says the result holds whether or not a condition is true. 凡……者均…… applies a rule to all members satisfying a description; 者 forms the expression for those members.
假若/假使 introduces a hypothesis. 幸亏/幸好……不然/否则…… contrasts an actual fortunate circumstance with an avoided bad outcome. 纵然/纵使……也…… maintains a result even under the conceded hypothetical condition.
（因）……故…… gives a compact, formal cause–result relationship. 以至(于) introduces an outcome reached because of the preceding situation, often at a notable or extreme extent.

These patterns build an argument from one case to another. 尚且……何况…… means 'even ... , let alone ...'. 连……都……更不用说…… extends an established strong case to a further conclusion. 别说……都/也…… and ……不说还…… add emphasis or another point; track which case is being asserted and which is used for comparison.
为(了)……起见 states the consideration motivating an action, 'for the sake of ...'. A following 以 clause can introduce the intended goal in formal writing: 'in order to ...'.

非得……才…… insists on a required condition or action before an outcome is possible. 任……也…… maintains the result regardless of the first circumstance. The second clause must be interpreted with the condition or concession in the first.

A multi-clause sentence contains more than one layer of logical relationships. First identify the main relationship, then work out how the smaller clauses express coordination, contrast, hypothesis, cause or progression within it.

Connected discourse organizes several sentences by time, space, reasoning or topic development. Topics can continue or shift; information may be omitted when earlier or later text makes its reference recoverable.
